source.title: Private Information Retrieval and Its Applications: An Introduction, Open Problems, Future Directions

accepted.question_text: For private read-update-write (PRUW), where a user downloads a chosen section of a data-storage system, updates it, and uploads the updates back without revealing the downloaded or uploaded content or their positions, and for PSU-based federated submodel learning (FSL), where private set union and symmetric private information retrieval are used so the server learns only the union or aggregate of submodels updated by clients rather than any individual client contribution, what are the fundamental converse limits on performance metrics such as read-write communication cost, and do those limits lead to capacity characterizations for PRUW and PSU-based FSL?
accepted.context_brief: Fundamental limits for PRUW and PSU-based FSL

evidence.quote: Private read-update-write (PRUW) [26]–[29] is the concept where a user downloads, updates and uploads the updates back to a chosen section of a data storage system, without revealing the content downloaded, uploaded or their positions, e.g., updated section index. PRUW is essentially the combination of private reading and private writing described previously.
The reading and writing costs are defined as the total number of bits downloaded and uploaded, normalized by the size of a submodel. The total cost is the sum of the reading and writing costs.

Therefore, [19] proposes a new private FSL approach which is based on PSU and SPIR. The core idea behind this scheme is to preserve client-side privacy by not allowing the server to learn any information beyond the subset of submodels (or the aggregation of updates of these submodels) collectively updated by the clients, i.e., the server learns nothing about any individual client’s contribution to the ultimate result.

Fundamental limits on performance metrics, i.e., converse results, have not yet been established for both PRUW and PSU based FSL. Investigating the fundamental limits is an interesting open problem, which might lead to capacity results of PRUW and PSU based FSL.

accepted.question_text: How can private read-write schemes for PRUW and PSU-based FSL be designed so that, in addition to preserving the intended private reading, private writing, and client-side privacy properties of those settings, they remain robust against adversaries and/or eavesdroppers?

evidence.quote: Private read-update-write (PRUW) [26]–[29] is the concept where a user downloads, updates and uploads the updates back to a chosen section of a data storage system, without revealing the content downloaded, uploaded or their positions, e.g., updated section index. PRUW is essentially the combination of private reading and private writing described previously.

Therefore, [19] proposes a new private FSL approach which is based on PSU and SPIR. The core idea behind this scheme is to preserve client-side privacy by not allowing the server to learn any information beyond the subset of submodels (or the aggregation of updates of these submodels) collectively updated by the clients, i.e., the server learns nothing about any individual client’s contribution to the ultimate result.
A practical and interesting future direction related to both PRUW and PSU based FSL is to develop private read-write schemes that are robust against adversaries or/and eavesdroppers.

accepted.question_text: Can PRUW be generalized from the existing single-client system model to a multi-client system model in which private read-write communication is defined for a group of clients, the same privacy, security, and correctness requirements are maintained, and communication cost is reduced by combining queries, answers, or updates from multiple clients?

evidence.quote: Private read-update-write (PRUW) [26]–[29] is the concept where a user downloads, updates and uploads the updates back to a chosen section of a data storage system, without revealing the content downloaded, uploaded or their positions, e.g., updated section index. PRUW is essentially the combination of private reading and private writing described previously.

All existing work on PRUW [26]–[28], [47], [48], [51], [52] consider a single client in the system model as shown in Fig. 9, i.e., all client-server communications are defined for a single client. A multi-client PRUW system model, where the private read-write process is defined from the perspective of a group of clients as opposed to defining it on an individual client with the same privacy, security and correctness requirements could be a promising future direction as it may result in a reduced communication cost, from combining queries/answers/updates of multiple clients.

accepted.question_text: In federated submodel learning, where a central learning model is divided into multiple submodels so each client downloads and updates only submodels relevant to that client’s local data, if a user has data for training multiple submodels at the same time, is there a private read/write method that lowers the total communication cost of reading and writing multiple submodels simultaneously compared with running the PRUW process separately for each submodel?
accepted.context_brief: Simultaneous private access to multiple FSL submodels

evidence.quote: One solution to this problem is federated submodel learning (FSL) [21]–[23], where the central learning model is divided into multiple submodels based on different types of training data, as this allows each client to only download and update the submodel(s) relevant to the client’s local data.

Private read-update-write (PRUW) [26]–[29] is the concept where a user downloads, updates and uploads the updates back to a chosen section of a data storage system, without revealing the content downloaded, uploaded or their positions, e.g., updated section index.

In a setting where a given user has a wide variety of data to train multiple submodels in FSL at the same time, it would be interesting to see if there exists any method that decreases the total communication cost of privately reading/writing to multiple submodels simultaneously, compared to carrying out the PRUW process on each submodel individually.

accepted.question_text: For PRUW in private federated learning or federated submodel learning with sparsification, how does the communication cost change if the privacy requirement is relaxed through a rate-privacy tradeoff, for example by incorporating differential privacy so that a specified amount of information may leak about the desired indices and the values of selected updates or parameters, rather than only about sparse-update indices as in existing rate-privacy-storage tradeoff work?
accepted.context_brief: Rate-privacy tradeoff for PRUW with sparsification

evidence.quote: In FL with top r sparsification, clients only download and upload the most significant r′ and r fractions of parameters and updates, respectively, to reduce the communication cost.

Motivated by these privacy concerns, the problem of PRUW in FL with top r sparsification is introduced in [26], [47], [48]. The privacy constraint on the downloaded (uploaded) parameter (update) indices requires the mutual information between the real indices and all the information received by an individual database to be equal to zero.

The rate-privacy-storage trade off in [48] only allows information to be leaked on the indices of the sparse updates in FL with sparsification, which does not have a significant impact on the communication rate. An interesting direction is to investigate the rate-privacy trade off in PRUW by incorporating differential privacy as in [4], [14] to see the effect on the communication cost in private FSL/FL with sparsification when allowing a given amount of information to be leaked on the desired indices as well as the values of the selected updates/parameters.

accepted.question_text: For private epidemiological data collection, a PRUW-related setting with users, databases, and a data collector and with both reading and writing components among those parties, what is the optimal writing cost, meaning the users’ upload cost, complementing prior work that considered the data collector’s download or reading cost?
accepted.context_brief: Writing cost in private epidemiological data collection

evidence.quote: Private read-update-write (PRUW) [26]–[29] is the concept where a user downloads, updates and uploads the updates back to a chosen section of a data storage system, without revealing the content downloaded, uploaded or their positions, e.g., updated section index.
The concept of PRUW can be used in other applications such as private epidemiological data collection.
problem is introduced in [53] which contains three parties, namely, users, databases and the data collector. The problem setting contains both reading and writing components among different parties.

The performance metric considered in [53] is the download cost at the data collector, i.e., the reading cost. An interesting future direction would be to consider the optimality of the writing cost, i.e., the upload cost of the users, which relates to the writing phase of PRUW.
